mainTopic: The end of the אבשלום section, reward for good deeds (מרים), and a verse-by-verse reading of the start of the slavery in מצרים.
overview: The גמרא finishes showing that אבשלום's revolt was part of הקב"ה's deep plan. It then explains that יוסף being sent 'from the valley of חברון' began the plan told to אברהם. It asks how אבשלום could say 'I have no son' and gives two answers: he had no son fit to be king, or his sons died because he burned יואב's field. Returning to the משנה, רבא concludes that good deeds are rewarded in the same way as the deed, but always more generously than punishment, as with מרים. רבי יצחק reads the פסוק about מרים watching משה as hinting at the שכינה. The גמרא then goes verse by verse through the start of the slavery in מצרים: the 'new king', פרעה's plan to drown the babies and how it backfired measure for measure, and the three advisors בלעם, איוב and יתרו. It also explains odd words such as 'him', 'over him', מסכנות, פיתום and רעמסס, and the future tense of 'he will multiply.' The amud ends by quoting the next פסוק, 'And the Egyptians made the children of Israel work', which is explained on the next amud.

steps.title: The verse that shows אבשלום's revolt was planned from above
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its earlier point with a פסוק: הקב"ה told דוד that evil would rise against him from his own house.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing an idea it started just before this section. It brings a פסוק to prove that אבשלום's revolt was part of a deep plan of הקב"ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just before this, the גמרא read 'the valley of the king' (עמק המלך) as 'the deep (עמוקה) plan of the King of the world.' This פסוק, from the נבואה of נתן to דוד, shows that trouble from inside דוד's own family was planned as a punishment. אבשלום was the one through whom it came true.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written; introduces a פסוק as proof

phrases.english: As it is written: 'Behold, I will raise up against you
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 12:11. ה׳ is speaking to דוד through נתן.

phrases.english: evil from your own house.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the drasha from just before this section, which read עמק המלך as the deep plan of the King of the world.
steps.raayaObject: That אבשלום's revolt was part of a deep plan of הקב"ה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל ב 12:11: 'I will raise up evil against you from your own house.'

steps.title: A similar case: יוסף sent from the 'depth' of Hebron
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר פפא reads 'the valley (עמק) of Hebron' as the deep (עמוקה) plan told to אברהם, who is buried in Hebron, that his children would be strangers in a foreign land.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the same way you can explain: 'And he sent him from the valley of Hebron.' רבי חנינא בר פפא said: from the deep plan of that צדיק who is buried in Hebron, as it is written: 'Know for sure that your children will be strangers.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a similar example. Just like 'the valley of the king' hinted at a deep plan, 'the valley of Hebron' in the story of יוסף hints at a deep plan too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hebron is on a hill, so 'valley of Hebron' looks strange. רבי חנינא בר פפא explains that עמק hints at עצה עמוקה, the deep plan told to אברהם at the ברית בין הבתרים. When יעקב sent יוסף to his brothers, he started the chain of events that brought the nation down to מצרים, just as that plan said.

keyTerms.meaning: In a similar way; introduces a parallel case
Your children will be strangers (in a foreign land)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a pattern the גמרא likes: a strange word in a פסוק can hint that events which look accidental are really part of הקב"ה's plan.

phrases.english: In a similar way you can say:
'And he sent him from the valley of Hebron,'
phrases.notes: בראשית 37:14. יעקב sends יוסף to check on his brothers.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa said:
from the deep plan of that righteous man
phrases.notes: He means אברהם, who is buried in מערת המכפלה in Hebron.

phrases.english: who is buried in Hebron,
as it is written: 'Know for sure'
that your children will be strangers.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a parallel to the עמק המלך drasha: another 'valley' that hints at a deep plan.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'The valley of Hebron' means the deep plan told to אברהם (buried in Hebron) that his children would go into exile. יוסף's trip began that plan.

steps.title: Didn't אבשלום have sons?
steps.stepSummary: אבשלום said 'I have no son,' but another פסוק says he had three sons and a daughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'For he said: I have no son.' But didn't he have sons? Isn't it written: 'And three sons and one daughter were born to אבשלום'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to אבשלום and points out two פסוקים that seem to contradict each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One פסוק says אבשלום built a monument because he had no son to carry his name. Another פסוק says he had three sons. The גמרא needs to explain how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written...? (opens a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: 'For he said: I have no son.'
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 18:18. This is why אבשלום set up a monument with his own name.

phrases.english: But didn't he have sons?
But isn't it written: 'And there were born to אבשלום
three sons and one daughter'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about אבשלום after finishing the deep-plan idea.
steps.kashyaTarget: The פסוק 'I have no son' (שמואל ב 18:18).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל ב 14:27 says clearly that אבשלום had three sons, so how could he say he had none?

steps.title: First answer: no son fit to be king
steps.stepSummary: רב יצחק בר אבדימי explains that אבשלום had sons, but none fit to be king.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יצחק בר אבדימי said: he meant that he had no son worthy of being king.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first answer to the contradiction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sons did exist, so the second פסוק is true. 'I have no son' means no son good enough to take over the kingdom, so in his eyes no one could carry on his name as king.

phrases.english: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi said:

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ בֵּן הָגוּן לַמַּלְכוּת.
phrases.english: That he did not have a son worthy of kingship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the meaning of the words 'I have no son'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'I have no son' means he had no children at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: He had sons, but none fit to be king.

steps.title: Second answer: his sons died because he burned יואב's field
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא brings a tradition: whoever burns another person's crops leaves no son to inherit him. אבשלום burned יואב's barley field, so his sons died.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: we have a tradition that anyone who burns his friend's crops will not leave a son to inherit him. And אבשלום burned יואב's crops, as it is written: 'He said to his servants: See, יואב's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire. And אבשלום's servants set the field on fire.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to the same contradiction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא says the sons really were born (like the earlier פסוק says) but later died. This was a punishment that fits the crime: he destroyed another man's 'produce', so he lost his own 'produce', his children. The פסוק about the burned field proves he did this sin.

keyTerms.meaning: We have learned it as a tradition

steps.confusionAlert: רב חסדא does not argue that the sons were never born. He means they were born and later died, so by the time of the monument אבשלום truly had no son.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: We have a tradition:
Anyone who burns the crops of his fellow
does not leave a son to inherit him.
And he burned the crops of Yoav,
as it is written: 'And he said to his servants:
See, Yoav's field is next to mine,
and he has barley there;
go and set it on fire.'
And Avshalom's servants set
the field on fire.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the contradiction in step 3, alongside רב יצחק בר אבדימי's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different times: the sons were born but later died as a punishment.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two פסוקים contradict each other about whether he had sons.
steps.terutzMaskana: He had sons, but they died because he burned יואב's field, so he was left without a son.

steps.title: How can one hour match seven days?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that good deeds are also rewarded measure for measure, using מרים as the example, and asks how one hour of waiting can be paid back with seven days.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'And the same is true for good, מרים etc.' Are these really alike? There it was one hour; here it was seven days!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back to the משנה's rule that good deeds are also paid back 'measure for measure', and challenges it from the משנה's own example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מרים waited a short time by the Nile to watch over baby משה. As a reward, the whole nation waited seven days for her when she had צרעת. If reward is exactly 'measure for measure', the reward should be the same size as the deed, but here it is much bigger.

keyTerms.meaning: Regarding good (the reward for good deeds)

phrases.english: 'And the same regarding good: Miriam, etc.'
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה. 'Etc.' points to the rest: she waited for משה, so the nation waited for her.

phrases.english: Are they comparable?
There, it was one hour;
phrases.notes: 'There' means מרים waiting by the river for משה.

phrases.english: here, it was seven days!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן לְעִנְיַן הַטּוֹבָה מִרְיָם וְכוּ׳. מִי דָּמֵי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אבשלום discussion and goes back to the משנה's rule about reward for good deeds.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's statement that good deeds are also paid 'measure for measure' (וכן לענין הטובה).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's own example does not match in size: one hour of waiting was rewarded with seven days of waiting.

steps.title: אביי: read the משנה as 'good is not like this'
steps.stepSummary: אביי suggests changing how we read the משנה: for good deeds it is not exactly measure for measure.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Say it like this: 'And regarding good, it is not so.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge by suggesting a different reading of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to אביי, the משנה is not saying good works the same way as punishment. It is saying good works differently: the reward is not limited to the size of the deed. That would explain why one hour earned seven days.

phrases.english: Abaye said: Say:
'And regarding good, it is not so.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by rereading the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה says good is paid exactly measure for measure, like punishment.
steps.terutzMaskana: Good is not paid exactly measure for measure; the reward can be bigger.

steps.title: רבא: the משנה clearly says 'and the same'
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects אביי's reading because the משנה plainly says 'and the same regarding good.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: But the משנה teaches 'and the same regarding good'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back against אביי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's reading flips the meaning of the words. The משנה says 'וכן', 'and the same', which means good is like punishment. You cannot read it as 'it is not so.'

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
But it teaches 'and the same regarding good'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: הָא ״וְכֵן לְעִנְיַן הַטּוֹבָה״ קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's answer in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: אביי's whole rereading of the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word 'וכן' ('and the same') says the opposite of 'it is not so.'

steps.title: רבא: same kind of reward, but good is always bigger
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the משנה: good is paid back in the same kind of way as the deed, but the reward for good is always bigger than punishment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said, this is what the משנה teaches: and the same is true for good, that it is paid back with the same measure. But the measure of good is always greater than the measure of punishment.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own answer to the 'one hour vs. seven days' question, and this is the final word here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Measure for measure' means the reward matches the type of the deed: מרים waited for משה, so the nation waited for her. But it does not have to match the size. Since good is always paid more generously than punishment, one hour can earn seven days.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (rejects the earlier idea and gives a new one)

steps.whatToRemember: Reward for good deeds is 'measure for measure' in its type, but always bigger in size than punishment. That is why מרים's one hour of waiting earned seven days of the nation waiting for her.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Measure for measure' here does not mean equal in amount. It means the same kind of payback, while the amount of reward can be much greater.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said, this is what it teaches:
'And the same regarding good,'
that it is with the same measure,
phrases.notes: He means the same kind of payback as the deed, not the same amount.

phrases.english: but the measure of good is always
greater than the measure of punishment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting אביי's reading, רבא gives his own explanation of the משנה that answers step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining 'measure for measure' as the same type of payback, not the same size.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Measure for measure' means the reward must be equal in amount to the deed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The reward matches the type of the deed, but good is always given more generously than punishment.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Good deeds are rewarded in the same way as the deed, but in a bigger amount, since the measure of good is always greater than the measure of punishment.

steps.title: The whole verse about מרים hints at the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק says the entire פסוק 'and his sister stood afar off' is really speaking about the שכינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And his sister stood afar off.' רבי יצחק said: this whole פסוק was said about the שכינה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the פסוק about מרים waiting for משה, and רבי יצחק says every part of it hints at the שכינה. This sets up the word-by-word proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We just learned that מרים was rewarded for waiting for משה. רבי יצחק adds a second, deeper layer: the same words also describe the שכינה standing guard over משה. The proof for each word comes in the next step.

phrases.english: "And his sister stood afar off,"
Rabbi Yitzchak said:
This entire verse
was said in reference to the Divine Presence:

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: פָּסוּק זֶה כּוּלּוֹ עַל שֵׁם שְׁכִינָה נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the פסוק about מרים from step 6 and reads it in a new way.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק of מרים watching משה is entirely a hint to the שכינה watching over him.

steps.title: Word-by-word proof that each word points to the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: For each word of the פסוק, the גמרא brings another פסוק where the same kind of word is used about ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Stood': as it says, 'ה׳ came and stood.' 'His sister': 'Say to wisdom, you are my sister.' 'Afar off': 'From afar ה׳ appeared to me.' 'To know': 'ה׳ is a God of knowledge.' 'What': 'What does ה׳ your God ask of you.' 'Would be done': 'ה׳ God will not do anything.' 'To him': 'ה׳ said to him, peace.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes through the פסוק one word at a time. For each word it shows another פסוק where that word is linked to ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the proof for רבי יצחק's claim. Each word of the מרים פסוק has a matching word in a פסוק about ה׳, so the whole פסוק can be read as the שכינה watching משה.

phrases.english: "And stood" — as it is written:
"And the Lord came, and stood, etc."
"His sister" — as it is written:
"Say to wisdom: You are my sister."
"Afar off" — as it is written:
"From afar the Lord appeared to me."
"To know" — as it is written:
phrases.notes: From here on, the words come from the rest of the same פסוק: 'to know what would be done to him.'

phrases.english: "For the Lord is a God of knowledge."
"What" — as it is written:
"What does the Lord your God ask of you."
"Would be done" — as it is written:
"For the Lord God will not do anything."
"To him" — as it is written:
"And the Lord said to him: Peace."

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יצחק reads the מרים פסוק on two levels: מרים watched משה, and the שכינה watched him too.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the proof for רבי יצחק's claim in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: That each word of the פסוק refers to the שכינה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Seven other פסוקים where the same words are used about ה׳.

steps.title: Was the 'new king' really new?
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל argue: one says it was truly a new king, the other says it was the same king with new decrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And a new king arose.' רב and שמואל: one said he was really new; the other said his decrees became new.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts learning the פסוקים about the slavery in מצרים. רב and שמואל disagree about what 'new king' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One opinion takes 'new' simply: a different person became king. The other says it was the same פרעה, who acted like a new king because he made new, harsh decrees. The reasons for each side come next.

phrases.english: "And there arose a new king, etc."
Rav and Shmuel:
One said: actually new,
and one said: that his decrees were made new.

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not tell us which one, רב or שמואל, holds which view. 'One said... one said' is all we get.
steps.triggerLanguage: רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל, חַד אָמַר: חָדָשׁ מַמָּשׁ, וְחַד אָמַר: שֶׁנִּתְחַדְּשׁוּ גְּזֵירוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the פסוקים about the slavery in מצרים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dispute: the king was truly new, or the same king with new decrees.

steps.title: The reasons behind each opinion
steps.stepSummary: One side relies on the word 'new'; the other notes the תורה never says the old king died.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says really new: because it says 'new.' The one who says new decrees: because it does not say 'he died and he reigned.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what each side in the argument is basing itself on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first view simply reads the word 'new.' The second view points out that the תורה does not write that the old king died and someone else took over, so it must be the same king who changed his policies.

keyTerms.meaning: and he died and he reigned

phrases.english: The one who says actually new —
because it is written "new,"
and the one who says his decrees were made new —
because it is not written "and he died, and he reigned."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning for both sides of the dispute in step 12.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word 'חָדָשׁ' for one side; the missing 'וַיָּמׇת וַיִּמְלוֹךְ' for the other.

steps.title: How the same king 'did not know יוסף'
steps.stepSummary: According to the 'new decrees' view, 'did not know יוסף' means he acted as if he never knew him.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Who did not know יוסף': he was like someone who did not know him at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the end of the פסוק according to the view that it was the same king.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If it was the same פרעה, he surely knew יוסף, so how can the פסוק say he did not know him? The answer: he acted like a stranger to יוסף, ignoring all the good יוסף had done.

phrases.english: "Who did not know Joseph,"
phrases.notes: This is explained according to the view that it was the same king, who surely knew יוסף.

phrases.english: that he was like
someone who did not know him at all.

steps.whatToRemember: According to the 'same king' view, פרעה pretended not to know יוסף and turned against his people.
steps.triggerLanguage: ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדַע אֶת יוֹסֵף״, דַּהֲוָה דָּמֵי כְּמַאן דְּלָא יָדַע לֵיהּ כְּלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the end of the פסוק ('who did not know יוסף') according to the 'new decrees' view from steps 12-13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the wording of the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Did not know יוסף' sounds like he truly never knew him, which fits only a new king.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means he acted as if he did not know יוסף, which fits the same king too.

steps.title: פרעה planned first, so he was struck first
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that since פרעה was the first to suggest the evil plan, he was the first to be punished.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he said to his people: Behold, the people of בני ישראל.' It was taught: he started the plan first, so he was struck first. He started first, as it says 'and he said to his people.' He was struck first, as it says 'on you, and on your people, and on all your servants.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that shows פרעה's punishment matched his crime. He came up with the plan before his people, and he was hit before his people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits the theme from earlier steps: מדה כנגד מדה, measure for measure. The proof for 'started first' is that פרעה spoke to his people. The proof for 'struck first' is that in the plague of frogs the פסוק lists פרעה ('you') before his people.

phrases.aramaic: ״וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל עַמּוֹ הִנֵּה עַם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״.
phrases.english: "And he said to his people: Behold, the people of the children of Israel."
It was taught:
He began with the plan first,
therefore he was struck first.
He began with the plan first —
as it is written: "And he said to his people,"
therefore he was struck first —
as it is written: "Both upon you, and upon your people, and upon all your servants."
phrases.notes: שמות 7:29, about the frogs. 'You' (פרעה) is listed first.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: הוּא הִתְחִיל בְּעֵצָה תְּחִילָּה לְפִיכָךְ לָקָה תְּחִילָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next פסוק in the story of the slavery.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פרעה started the evil plan first, so he was punished first.

steps.title: Why does פרעה say 'him' and not 'them'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק says 'let us deal wisely with him' when it is talking about the whole Jewish people.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Come, let us deal wisely with him.' It should have said 'with them'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a strange word in the פסוק. פרעה is talking about a whole nation, so he should have said 'them,' not 'him.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is about the wording. A singular word ('him') is used for a plural group (the Jews), so the גמרא assumes it must be hinting at someone specific. The answer comes next.

phrases.english: "Come, let us deal wisely with him."
It should have said "with them"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next פסוק and questions its wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: The singular word 'לוֹ' in the פסוק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: פרעה is speaking about the whole Jewish people, so the plural 'לָהֶם' would be expected.

steps.title: 'Him' means the Savior of ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא explains that 'him' refers to the One who saves ישראל, meaning ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא said: Come, let us outsmart the Savior of ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא answers the question. 'Him' is not the Jewish people; it is the One who saves them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The singular word now makes sense, because it points to one Being, ה׳. פרעה was plotting how to get around ה׳'s protection of ישראל. The next steps (18-19) explain how he planned to do this.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said:
Come and let us outsmart
the Savior of Israel —

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: בֹּאוּ וְנֶחְכַּם לְמוֹשִׁיעָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying a different subject for the singular word
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Him' should refer to the Jewish people, so it ought to be plural.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Him' refers to ה׳, the one Savior of ישראל, so the singular is correct.

steps.title: פרעה's advisors reject fire and sword
steps.stepSummary: The advisors ask which kind of death to use. They rule out fire and sword, because פסוקים show ה׳ punishes with those.
steps.simpleTranslation: With what should we judge them? With fire? It is written that ה׳ comes in fire and judges with fire. With the sword? It is written 'and with His sword against all flesh.'
steps.whatsHappening: פרעה's advisors are working out how to kill the Jewish people. They cross off fire and sword, which sets up the next step, where they choose water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The advisors are afraid of being paid back in the same way they act. Since ישעיהו describes ה׳ judging with fire and sword, they worry that using those would bring the same punishment back on them.

keyTerms.meaning: we will judge them (decide their punishment)

phrases.english: With what shall we judge them?
phrases.notes: These are פרעה's advisors talking about how to kill the Jewish people.

phrases.english: Shall we judge them with fire?
It is written: 'For behold, the Lord will come in fire,'
and it is written: 'For by fire will the Lord contend,' and so on.
With the sword?
It is written: 'And by His sword with all flesh.'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 66:16. The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the advisors' plan to 'deal wisely' against the One who saves ישראל by choosing a punishment ה׳ won't repay in kind.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which kind of death can be used without ה׳ paying them back the same way?

steps.title: The advisors choose water
steps.stepSummary: They decide on drowning, because ה׳ swore never to bring another מבול.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, let us judge them with water, because ה׳ already swore not to bring a flood on the world, as it says, 'For this is as the waters of נח to Me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The advisors answer their own question. Water is safe, they think, because of ה׳'s oath after the מבול.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their logic is: if ה׳ promised never to flood again, then He cannot punish them with water. So drowning the babies looks to them like a punishment with no comeback.

keyTerms.meaning: the Holy One, Blessed be He

phrases.english: Rather, let us come and judge them with water,
for the Holy One, Blessed be He, already swore
that He will not bring a flood upon the world,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״כִּי מֵי נֹחַ זֹאת לִי וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: as it is said: 'For this is as the waters of Noah to Me,' and so on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18 by choosing water.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Water, because ה׳ swore not to bring another flood.

steps.title: The flaw: the oath was only about the whole world
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the advisors missed something. ה׳ promised not to flood the whole world, but He can still bring water on one nation.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they did not know that He would not bring a flood on the whole world, yet on one nation He can bring it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps in to show why the advisors' plan was wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath was narrower than they thought. It covers only a flood of the whole world. A water punishment on just the מצרים is still possible.

phrases.english: But they did not know

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁעַל כׇּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ אֵינוֹ מֵבִיא,
phrases.english: that upon the entire world He does not bring it,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל עַל אוּמָּה אַחַת הוּא מֵבִיא.
phrases.english: but upon one nation He does bring it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reasoning of step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The advisors' belief that water was safe.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The oath was limited to a worldwide flood, not a flood on one nation.

steps.title: A second flaw: they could run into the water themselves
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: ה׳ doesn't bring the water on them, but they go into it on their own, as the פסוק says, 'and מצרים fled toward it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Alternatively: He does not bring it, but they come and fall into it. And so it says, 'And the Egyptians fled toward it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way the advisors' plan fails, and brings a פסוק from קריעת ים סוף to show it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if ה׳'s oath stopped Him from bringing water on them, the oath says nothing about people running into water themselves. At the ים סוף the מצרים ran toward the sea, so the oath was never broken.

phrases.english: Alternatively: He does not bring it,
but they come and fall into it.
And so it says: 'And the Egyptians fled toward it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second reason, beside step 20, why the water plan failed.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The advisors' belief that water was safe.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The oath doesn't cover people who go into the water by themselves.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: they were cooked in their own pot
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads 'בדבר אשר זדו עליהם' to mean that the מצרים were punished with the same thing they did: water.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי אלעזר said: What does 'for in the matter in which they plotted against them' mean? In the pot in which they cooked, they themselves were cooked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from רבי אלעזר that the מצרים were punished with water, measure for measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר reads 'זדו' as cooking. The מצרים 'cooked' the Jewish babies in water, so they were 'cooked' in water at the sea. This matches the water punishment from the step before.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is what [he] said: brings support

phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: מַאי דִּכְתִיב ״כִּי בַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר זָדוּ עֲלֵיהֶם״ —
phrases.english: What is meant by that which is written: 'For in the matter in which they plotted against them'?
In the pot in which they cooked, in it they were cooked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the idea that the מצרים were punished through water.
steps.raayaObject: That the מצרים were punished with water for drowning the babies.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אלעזר's reading of 'אשר זדו עליהם'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a clear example of מדה כנגד מדה, the theme running through this whole part of the גמרא.

steps.title: How do we know 'זדו' means cooking?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for proof that the word 'זדו' has to do with a pot.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where can we tell that this word 'זדו' is a word for a pot?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks רבי אלעזר's reading and asks where the cooking meaning comes from. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually 'זדו' sounds like 'acting on purpose' or 'plotting.' The גמרא wants a source for reading it as cooking.

keyTerms.meaning: from where can it be understood?

phrases.english: From where can it be understood that this word 'zadu'
is a term for a pot?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind רבי אלעזר's reading.

steps.title: Proof from יעקב's cooking
steps.stepSummary: The same root appears in 'ויזד יעקב נזיד', where יעקב cooked a pot of stew.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And יעקב cooked a stew.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק where the same root clearly means cooking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In 'ויזד יעקב נזיד' the root זיד plainly means cooking. So 'זדו' can carry that meaning too.
steps.whatToRemember: The מצרים drowned the Jewish babies, so they were drowned themselves. 'In the pot they cooked in, they were cooked.'

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And Jacob cooked a stew.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The root זיד means cooking, as in 'ויזד יעקב נזיד'.

steps.title: Three people were in פרעה's council
steps.stepSummary: רבי סימאי teaches that בלעם, איוב and יתרו were part of פרעה's council about the Jewish people.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי סימאי: Three were in that council: בלעם, איוב and יתרו.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement opens. It names three people who were in פרעה's planning council.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opens a new part of the story. The three names set up a discussion of what each of them did in that council and what happened to each one.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי סִימַאי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Simai:
Three were in that council:
Balaam, and Job, and Yitro.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי סִימַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about who was in פרעה's council.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בלעם, איוב and יתרו took part in פרעה's council.

steps.title: What happened to each of the three advisors
steps.stepSummary: בלעם, who advised, was killed. איוב, who was silent, suffered. יתרו, who ran away, merited grandchildren in the לשכת הגזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: בלעם gave the advice, so he was killed. איוב kept quiet, so he was punished with suffering. יתרו ran away, so some of his descendants earned a seat in the לשכת הגזית.
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching from the last step continues. Now we hear what happened to each of the three advisors in פרעה's council.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each advisor gets a result that matches what he did. The one who pushed for the evil plan was killed. The one who stayed quiet suffered, and the one who protested by running away was rewarded with honor for his family.

keyTerms.meaning: the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the סנהדרין sat

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches that staying silent in the face of evil is also judged. It is not as bad as giving the evil advice, but it is far from what יתרו did when he protested.

phrases.english: Bilaam, who advised, was killed;
phrases.notes: במדבר 31:8 tells how he was killed.

phrases.english: Iyov, who was silent, was punished with suffering.
Yitro, who ran away,
merited that some of his children's children
sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the statement about the three advisors by telling what happened to each.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each advisor was paid back according to his response: death, suffering, or reward.

steps.title: Proof that יתרו's descendants became scholars
steps.stepSummary: Two פסוקים show that the קינים, יתרו's family, were families of scribes.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the פסוק says, 'The families of scribes who lived at יעבץ... these are the קינים.' Another פסוק says, 'The children of the קיני, the father-in-law of משה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings פסוקים to prove what it just said about יתרו's reward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק calls the קינים 'families of scribes,' meaning Torah scholars. The second פסוק shows that the קיני was משה's father-in-law, which is יתרו. Put the two together, and you see that יתרו's descendants became scholars fit to sit in the סנהדרין.

keyTerms.meaning: the Kenite, a name for יתרו's family

phrases.english: as it is stated:
"And the families of scribes who dwelt at Yabetz,
Tirathites, Shimeathites, Sucathites,
these are the Kenites who came from Chammat,
the father of the house of Rechav."
And it is written: "And the children of the Kenite, Moshe's father-in-law, etc."
phrases.notes: שופטים 1:16. This is the link showing that the קינים are יתרו's family.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for יתרו's reward.
steps.raayaObject: That יתרו's descendants became great scholars
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברי הימים א 2:55 together with שופטים 1:16
steps.whatToRemember: בלעם advised and was killed. איוב was silent and suffered. יתרו ran away, and his grandchildren became scholars.

steps.title: Why does the פסוק say 'he will go up from the land'?
steps.stepSummary: פרעה feared the Jews would drive the Egyptians out, so the פסוק should have said 'and we will go up.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says the Jews will 'fight against us and go up from the land.' It should have said 'and we will go up'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the end of the same פסוק as 'הבה נתחכמה לו' (שמות 1:10). It points out that one word seems wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Jews joined Egypt's enemies and won, the Egyptians would be the ones forced out of the land, not the Jews. So the word 'ועלה' (he will go up) does not fit what פרעה was afraid of.

keyTerms.meaning: and he will go up from the land

phrases.english: "And he will fight against us and go up from the land";
it should have said "and we will go up"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by looking closely at the wording of שמות 1:10.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: פרעה's real fear was that the Egyptians would be driven out, so the פסוק should speak of 'us.'

steps.title: פרעה hung his own curse on someone else
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר כהנא explains that פרעה was like a person who curses himself but says it about his friend.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר כהנא said: It is like a person who curses himself but hangs the curse on his friend.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא בר כהנא answers the question about the odd word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פרעה really meant that the Egyptians would be driven out. He did not want to say something bad about himself, so he phrased it as if it would happen to the Jews.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said:
It is like a person who curses himself
and hangs his curse on his friend.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר כָּהֲנָא כְּאָדָם שֶׁמְּקַלֵּל אֶת עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the wording as a polite way of speaking
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק should have said 'we,' since the danger was to the Egyptians.
steps.terutzMaskana: פרעה meant 'we' but put his own bad outcome on the Jews.

steps.title: Why does the פסוק say 'over him' instead of 'over them'?
steps.stepSummary: The taskmasters were set over the Jews, a plural group, so 'עליו' (over him) seems wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'they placed taskmasters over him.' It should have said 'over them'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא looks at the next פסוק and again points out a word that seems off.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The taskmasters ruled over all of בני ישראל, so we would expect the plural 'עליהם.' The singular 'עליו' suggests the פסוק means a particular 'him.'

phrases.english: "And they placed taskmasters over him";
it should have said "over them"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same kind of wording question, now on שמות 1:11.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A singular word is used for a whole nation.

steps.title: The brick mold on פרעה's neck
steps.stepSummary: The 'him' is פרעה. The Egyptians hung a brick mold on his neck so that no Jew could refuse to work.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון taught: They brought a brick mold and hung it on פרעה's neck. Whenever a Jew said 'I'm too delicate for this,' they answered him: 'Are you more delicate than פרעה?'
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא answers the question by explaining who 'him' is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Him' means פרעה. The work was first placed on פרעה himself, as a show to make it look like everyone was joining in. This took away every excuse, and that is how the Jews were tricked into slavery.

keyTerms.meaning: it was taught in the study hall of

phrases.aramaic: תָּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן:
phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon taught:
This teaches that they brought a brick mold
and hung it on Pharaoh's neck,
and each and every one of Israel
who said to them, "I am delicate,"
they said to him:
Are you at all more delicate than Pharaoh?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן מְלַמֵּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about 'עליו.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Him' should refer to the Jewish people, so it should be plural.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Him' is פרעה, who carried a brick mold as a trick.
steps.confusionAlert: פרעה did not really become a worker. The brick mold was a show to trick the Jews into agreeing to work.

steps.title: The meaning of the name 'שרי מסים'
steps.stepSummary: 'מסים' is read as 'משים,' meaning something that makes people produce bricks.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'שרי מסים' means officers over something that forces the making of bricks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the name 'שרי מסים' from the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא connects the word 'מסים' to 'משים,' which means making or putting. The taskmasters were the ones who forced the Jews to produce bricks.

phrases.english: "Sarei missim" (taskmasters):
something that makes them produce (bricks).
phrases.notes: It's a play on sounds: מסים sounds like משים. Some versions leave out the word in round brackets.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains another word from the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'מסים' comes from 'משים,' meaning forcing the production of bricks.
steps.whatToRemember: Two odd words: 'ועלה' shows פרעה hanging his own curse on the Jews, and 'עליו' shows the brick mold trick on פרעה's neck.

steps.title: Why does the verse say 'to afflict him' instead of 'them'?
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says 'ענותו' (to afflict him), but the Jews are many people, so it should say 'ענותם' (to afflict them).
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'in order to afflict him with their burdens.' It should have said 'to afflict them'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices a wording problem: the פסוק uses a singular word for the Jews, who are a large group.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The burdens are called 'their' burdens, which is plural. So the word for who is being afflicted should also be plural. The singular 'him' looks out of place, and the next step will explain it.

phrases.english: "In order to afflict him with their burdens"
It should have said "to afflict them"!
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same kind of wording problem as Step 30, now on the next words of the פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The singular word ענותו in שמות 1:11.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The burdens are plural ('their'), so the people being afflicted should also be plural.

steps.title: 'Him' means פרעה, who was given the Jews' burden as a show
steps.stepSummary: The 'him' is פרעה. He was given the Jews' kind of burden, the brick mold, as a show to draw the Jews into the work.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means: in order to afflict פרעה, through the burdens of the Jewish people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'him' means פרעה, the same idea it used in Step 31.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 31 said the Egyptians hung a brick mold on פרעה's neck. So the 'affliction' in the פסוק is on פרעה himself, and 'their burdens' are the burdens placed on ישראל. Both words now fit: 'him' is singular because it means פרעה, and 'their' is plural because it means the Jews.

keyTerms.meaning: to פרעה, meaning aimed at פרעה

phrases.english: In order to afflict him, meaning Pharaoh,
phrases.notes: This goes back to Step 31, where the Egyptians hung a brick mold on פרעה's neck.

phrases.english: through the burdens of the Jewish people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of who the pronoun refers to
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Him' must refer to the Jewish people, so it should have been plural.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Him' refers to פרעה, and 'their burdens' refers to ישראל.

steps.title: מסכנות: cities that endanger their owners
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל explain the word מסכנות. The first opinion: these were buildings that put their owners in danger.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And they built storage cities for פרעה.' רב and שמואל disagree. One says: these are cities that endanger their owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next words of the פסוק and starts a disagreement between רב and שמואל about the word מסכנות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion reads מסכנות as coming from סכנה, meaning danger. These cities were risky for the people who owned them. The second opinion comes in the next step.

phrases.english: "And they built storage cities for Pharaoh"
Rav and Shmuel disagree:
One says: they are cities that endanger their owners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next phrase in the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מסכנות means buildings that are dangerous for their owners.

steps.title: מסכנות: cities that make their owners poor
steps.stepSummary: The second opinion: מסכנות means buildings that make their owners poor, because building costs so much.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other one says: these are cities that impoverish their owners, as the Master said: anyone who busies himself with building becomes poor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second side of the disagreement and backs it up with a well-known saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opinion reads מסכנות as coming from מסכן, a poor person. To support it, the גמרא quotes a known teaching that construction drains a person's money. So the name tells us these cities cost their owners a lot.

keyTerms.meaning: as the Master said (quoting a known teaching)
one who busies himself with building

phrases.english: And one says: they are cities that impoverish their owners,
as the Master said:
Anyone who busies himself with building becomes poor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the disagreement begun in Step 35.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מסכנות means buildings that make their owners poor, supported by the teaching that building makes a person poor.

steps.title: The city's real name was פיתום; רעמסס means it kept collapsing
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל disagree about the two names. One says the real name was פיתום, and it was also called רעמסס because its buildings kept falling down one after another.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'פיתום and רעמסס.' רב and שמואל disagree. One says: its name was פיתום. Why was it called רעמסס? Because each building, one after another, would collapse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the city names in the פסוק, with רב and שמואל again giving two opinions. This is the first one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions treat פיתום and רעמסס as one city with a main name and a nickname. Here פיתום is the real name, and רעמסס is a nickname that sounds like מתרוסס, 'crumbling.' The buildings kept falling apart one after another.
steps.confusionAlert: The פסוק sounds like it names two cities, but here both רב and שמואל are talking about ONE city with two names. The only question is which name is the real one and which is a nickname.

phrases.english: "Pithom and Raamses."
Rav and Shmuel disagree:
One says: Pithom is its name,
and why was it called Raamses?
Because each building, one after another, would collapse.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל, חַד אָמַר: פִּיתוֹם שְׁמָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the last words of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The city's real name was פיתום. It was nicknamed רעמסס because its buildings kept collapsing.

steps.title: The city's real name was רעמסס; פיתום means the abyss swallowed it
steps.stepSummary: The other opinion says the real name was רעמסס. It was nicknamed פיתום because the mouth of the deep (פי תהום) swallowed each building.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one says: its name was רעמסס. Why was it called פיתום? Because the mouth of the deep swallowed each building, one after another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second opinion, which flips which name is the real one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now רעמסס is the main name, and פיתום is read as two words, פי תהום, 'mouth of the deep.' The buildings sank into the ground one by one. Both opinions agree the Jews' building work kept failing; they only disagree about which name carries that message.

keyTerms.meaning: mouth of the deep, the abyss

steps.whatToRemember: Each phrase of the פסוק is being read for a hidden message about the slavery: מסכנות shows danger or poverty, and the names פיתום and רעמסס show buildings that collapsed or sank.

phrases.english: And one says: Raamses is its name,
and why was it called Pithom?
Because the mouth of the deep swallowed each building, one after another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The other side of the disagreement from Step 37.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The city's real name was רעמסס. It was nicknamed פיתום because the deep swallowed its buildings.

steps.title: Why does the verse use the future tense?
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says 'he will multiply and he will spread' in the future tense. It is describing the past, so it should have said 'they multiplied and they spread.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'But as much as they afflicted him, so he will multiply and so he will spread.' It should have said 'so they multiplied and so they spread'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next פסוק and points out a tense problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is telling a story about what already happened in מצרים, so past tense would be expected. Instead it uses the future tense, יִרְבֶּה and יִפְרוֹץ. The גמרא asks why.

phrases.english: "But as much as they afflicted him,
so he will multiply and so he will spread."
It should have said "so they multiplied and so they spread"!

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּן רַבּוּ וְכֵן פָּרְצוּ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next פסוק with a new wording question.
steps.kashyaTarget: The future tense of יִרְבֶּה and יִפְרוֹץ in שמות 1:12.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A story about the past should be told in the past tense.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: רוח הקודש was announcing the future
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains that these words were a message from רוח הקודש to the Egyptians: the more you afflict them, the more they will grow.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: רוח הקודש was announcing to them: 'so he will multiply and so he will spread.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש answers the tense question: the words are a prophecy, so they are said in the future tense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words are not just the narrator describing the past. They are what רוח הקודש told the Egyptians would happen. That is why the future tense fits: 'the more you afflict them, the more they will grow.'

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Divine inspiration was announcing to them:
"So he will multiply and so he will spread."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ מְבַשַּׂרְתָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 39.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes who is speaking: the words are a prophecy, not the narrator's description
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The words describe what already happened, so they should be past tense.
steps.terutzMaskana: The words are a message from רוח הקודש about the future, so the future tense is correct.

steps.title: ויקצו: the Jews looked like thorns to the Egyptians
steps.stepSummary: The word ויקצו hints at קוצים, thorns. The Egyptians saw the Jews as thorns.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And they were disgusted because of the children of Israel.' This teaches that the Jews looked like thorns in their eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next word in the פסוק, ויקצו, by connecting it to the word for thorns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ויקצו normally means 'they were disgusted.' The גמרא reads it as related to קוצים, thorns. The Egyptians saw the growing Jewish nation as something painful and annoying, like thorns.

phrases.english: "And they were disgusted because of the children of Israel"
This teaches that they appeared
in their eyes like thorns.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues with the next words of the same פסוק discussed in Steps 39-40.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ויקצו is connected to קוצים: the Egyptians saw the Jews as thorns.

steps.title: Quoting the next verse about the slavery
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to the next פסוק in the slavery story: 'And the Egyptians made the children of Israel work.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The next פסוק says: "And the Egyptians made the children of Israel work."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is only quoting the next פסוק here. It is setting up the next move, where it will explain something in this פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 39-41 explained words in the previous פסוקים one by one. Now the גמרא keeps the same pattern and moves on to the next line of the story. Nothing has been taught yet. This line just tells us which words the coming explanation is about.

keyTerms.meaning: And they made [them] work, or enslaved
The children of Israel, the Jewish people

phrases.english: "And the Egyptians made work
phrases.notes: This is שמות 1:13, the next פסוק after the ones the גמרא was just explaining.

phrases.english: the children of Israel

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the previous פסוק (ויקצו, step 41) to the next פסוק in the slavery story, keeping the same verse-by-verse pattern.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No teaching yet. The פסוק is quoted to introduce the next explanation.
